title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Two Courts Met
moral: When you build a bridge between worlds, you discover that the worlds were never as far apart as everyone believed.

pages.content:
The Royal Palace of Veradine sat on a hill above a forest, and the forest sat on top of one of the oldest fairy territories on the continent, and for three hundred years these two facts had produced a complicated silence between two courts that occupied the same geography without acknowledging each other.

The silence had been broken, on this particular evening, by accident. A peace summit between the courts had been scheduled for midsummer, and the invitations had been sent, and they had crossed in the post, and now both courts had arrived expecting to be the host rather than the guest, and no one had planned for the situation where both courts occupied the grand hall at the same time.

{{NAME}} was there as the human representative, which was a role that had been invented twenty minutes ago when someone needed a third party and he happened to be passing. He stood in the doorway of the grand hall and took in the scene: on one side, the fairy court in its full luminous assembly, hundreds of them arranged by rank in the air above the eastern half of the hall. On the other side, the royal court of Veradine in formal dress, every face very carefully neutral. In the centre, a vast and eloquent empty space.

{{NAME}} straightened his jacket and walked into the empty space.

pages.content:
The Fairy Chamberlain and the Royal Chancellor both turned toward {{NAME}} simultaneously, and both opened their mouths to say, in their respective capacities, that he had no authority to be in the centre of anything.

{{NAME}} had anticipated this. He had the kind of mind that anticipated things of this kind.

'I'm the new representative for the middle ground,' he said calmly, which was not technically a lie because it had not existed before and therefore had no previous representative. 'And I think we should start with something small. Can both courts agree that this hall has excellent windows?'

There was a pause of precisely the right length.

From the fairy side, a court fairy with wings like hammered emerald and an expression of permanent sceptical assessment hovered forward. Her name was Wren and she had been the most difficult voice in the fairy court for forty years, which meant she was the most important voice to have on any agreement.

'The windows are acceptable,' Wren said.

Behind {{NAME}}, the Royal Chancellor said, very carefully: 'We are in agreement about the windows.'

{{NAME}}'s eyes met Princess Lira's across the empty space. She was about his age, in the Veradine royal party, and she had been watching him with an expression of very quiet, very focused interest. She gave him the smallest possible nod.

pages.content:
What followed was the most extraordinary evening of diplomatic improvisation {{NAME}} had ever conducted, which was all the evenings of diplomatic improvisation he had conducted, because he had never conducted any before and was therefore, paradoxically, unencumbered by preconceptions about how it was supposed to go.

He moved between the courts with Princess Lira at his side and Wren hovering at his shoulder, and he found things they had in common and brought them forward: both courts kept the same festival in autumn, with different names. Both courts considered the central forest ancient and inviolable. Both courts had a tradition of songs passed down without written notation, which had led to independent variations that, when Wren's court sang them alongside Lira's court musicians, produced something neither of them had ever heard before.

The hall filled with it, this unexpected harmonic, and it did something to the empty space in the centre. It made it smaller. Not the space between them: the version of the space in everyone's heads, the one that had been three hundred years in the making.

Wren had not stopped hovering forward since the windows. Lira had not looked at the fairy court with wariness since the second song.

pages.content:
The agreement they reached was not a formal treaty. Formal treaties, {{NAME}} had observed, required everyone to leave as quickly as possible in order to tell other people they had been at a formal treaty, which rather defeated the purpose.

This was something more durable: both courts agreeing to use the forest together on alternate festivals, beginning with the autumn one. Both courts agreeing to teach the song to each other's young, with all its variations. Wren agreeing, with the careful dignity of someone making a concession they have in fact wanted to make for a long time, to open the fairy paths through the forest to the palace's north wing.

The hardest part had not been the courts. The hardest part had been the moment, twenty minutes into the evening, when {{NAME}} had been certain it was going to fall apart, when Wren and the Royal Chancellor had both retreated toward their respective sides, and he had simply stood in the empty centre and waited, very quietly, for the silence to become more uncomfortable for everyone else than the alternative.

It had taken four minutes. In four minutes both of them had come back.

Lira stood beside him at the centre of the hall now and looked around at what had happened and said, quietly: 'How did you know it would work?'

'I didn't,' he said honestly. 'But the middle ground was available.'

pages.content:
The grand hall emptied gradually as both courts found each other's company more comfortable than they had expected, and the conversations moved out through the palace and into the forest paths and eventually into a kind of companionable quiet that did not require conversation at all.

{{NAME}} sat on the grand hall's wide windowsill with his back against the frame. Wren had folded her hammered-emerald wings for the first time all evening and sat on the windowsill beside him, which {{NAME}} understood to be a significant event. Lira sat on his other side, shoes off, feet tucked up, a piece of fairy court scroll she had been given unrolling in her lap.

Below the window, the forest was alive with the quiet conversation of the two courts finding the beginning of something new in the dark between the trees.

{{NAME}}'s bridge brooch caught the light from below, and Wren looked at it, and then at him, with an expression that said several things without saying any of them.

His eyes grew warm and slow. Outside, the forest hummed.

Goodnight, bridge-builder. Dream of open middle ground, and wonder what the two courts might discover next time they meet.
